title: Acoustic Design Criteria in Naturally Ventilated Residential Buildings: New Research Perspectives by Applying the Indoor Soundscape Approach

findings.antecedent: External noise intrusion via ventilation openings
findings.consequent: Use of natural ventilation (NV) in buildings
findings.quote: The indoor-outdoor connection they provide has been, so far, a major limiting factor in the use of NV due to the conflict between ventilation needs and the intrusion of external noise, which impedes naturally ventilated buildings from meeting background noise limits set by acoustic standards, building design regulations and rating protocols.

findings.antecedent: Traditional noise control engineering approach (minimizing sound levels)
findings.consequent: Holistic consideration of Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ) needs (ventilation, visual, cooling, acoustic)
findings.quote: First, a fragmented view towards indoor environmental quality has not included consideration of the following acoustic criteria: (i) how buildings are designed and operated to meet multiple needs other than acoustical ones (e.g., ventilation, visual, and cooling needs) and (ii) how people respond to multiple simultaneous environmental factors.

findings.antecedent: Lack of a perceptual perspective in acoustic criteria
findings.consequent: Consideration of multiple cognitive and behavioral factors (e.g., connection with outside, sense of control) impinging on comfort in naturally ventilated houses
findings.quote: Secondly, the lack of a perceptual perspective has led acoustic criteria to neglect the multiple cognitive and behavioral factors impinging on comfort in naturally ventilated houses.

findings.antecedent: Connection with the outside and sense of control over one's environment
findings.consequent: Opportunities for 'adaptive acoustic comfort' (higher noise tolerance)
findings.quote: Indeed, factors such as the connection with the outside and the sense of control over one's environment may induce “adaptive acoustic comfort" opportunities that are worth investigating.

findings.antecedent: Various façade noise control solutions (passive, active, automation-based, hybrid)
findings.consequent: Large-scale adoption in naturally ventilated buildings
findings.quote: Even if research on this topic is continuously ongoing and some solutions seem to be more promising than others, currently, none of the reviewed techniques fully satisfy the stated needs and none have been adopted on a large scale.

findings.antecedent: Better indoor thermal and air quality conditions (e.g., for overheating mitigation)
findings.consequent: Tolerance of higher indoor noise levels from transportation sources in NV buildings
findings.quote: The draft Acoustics Ventilation and Overheating Residential Design Guide (hereinafter AVO guide), produced by the Association of Noise Consultants in the UK, allows for higher levels of indoor noise from transportation sources when higher ventilation rates are needed to mitigate overheating, for example, by window opening, based on the following assumptions: (i) overheating occurs only for short periods of the year, (ii) suboptimal acoustic conditions are bearable when counterbalanced by better indoor thermal and air quality conditions, and (iii) occupants are provided with some control over their environment [79,81].

findings.consequent: Full characterization of perceived sound quality (e.g., pleasantness ratings) and comfort
findings.quote: The literature has already reported numerous criticisms on the effectiveness of decibel-based metrics in fully characterizing perceived sound quality (e.g., pleasantness ratings) [51].
In this perspective, sounds can be unwanted or wanted, and as such a “resource" to be exploited for generating positive indoor soundscapes according to people preference [44].
